Chapter 7
Integrating with Plant Maintenance
When integrating QM in the logistics and supply chain management
processes, you need to take great care with test equipment that you use
to conduct various quality tests. You can broaden the QM scope by inte-
grating test equipment management into the business functions of
plant maintenance.
Building on the functions of plant maintenance (PM) and quality management (QM),
SAP S/4HANA provides integrated test equipment management that combines
important planning and processing functions of PM and QM. You should therefore
view the combination of the planning and processing functions not as a separate area,
but as an operating interface that combines the appropriate functions of the different
areas for test equipment management and monitoring to facilitate business users
meeting their business needs.
It’s essential that all quality inspections and quality tests be undertaken using reliable
test equipment and measuring devices that give accurate results. For this reason, test
equipment management and its calibration are of paramount importance.
Equipment or functional locations are defined as PM master data. A piece of equipment
can be a boiler, a condenser, or a chiller, while a functional location can be a utility room
or chiller room of a manufacturing plant. The steps to integrate QM with any of PM’s
equipment or functional locations are the same that we show for test equipment man-
agement in this chapter. Test equipment can be specific laboratory equipment such as a
weighing scale that is used to conduct physical or chemical quality tests of materials.
Note
In this chapter, we’ll describe the functionality of PM in sufficient detail for the pur-
poses of test equipment management; however, we can’t cover every possible busi-
ness scenario. We’ll restrict the scope of this chapter to typical and routine business
processes that use PM, QM, and materials management (MM). Due to the integrated
nature of QM with other areas, it’s always best to coordinate with experts or consul-
tants of other SAP areas to ensure meeting end-to-end business scenarios of a client
where SAP S/4HANA is being implemented.
The business process requires that you fulfill the requirements of managing the
monitoring of test equipment according to relevant quality standards. To do this, the

7 Integrating with Plant Maintenance
324
monitoring and test equipment (referred to as test equipment in the rest of this chap-
ter) requires that you maintain detailed data on device type, usage site, inspection
frequency, inspection method, and acceptance criteria, as well as measures to take in
case of unsatisfactory results. In addition, the business requirement is to list, evalu-
ate, and make available the inspection results for the test equipment. The SAP system
can meet the standard requirements.
Note
Given its very high importance in ensuring business continuity, you’ll find test equip-
ment management in SAP via menu path Logistics  Quality Management  Test Equip-
ment Management.
We’ll start this chapter with the factors that you need to consider to help you decide
which SAP S/4HANA system areas you need to implement to map the business pro-
cesses of PM. Next, we’ll cover the configuration basics of the serial number profile that
you’ll need for equipment, and then delve into covering the important master data
required to run the business processes. We’ll also cover the business processes of QM
integration with PM and will also discuss some PM reports available in the system.
Finally, we’ll also discuss an end-to-end setup to successfully create an inspection
checklist, which is a new functionality available in SAP S/4HANA 2023.
7.1 Deciding which Functionalities to Implement
As already mentioned, apart from the central role that the QM plays, two other areas of
SAP S/4HANA that contribute significantly to test equipment management business
processes are PM and MM. Figure 7.1 shows the four possible business scenarios in
which you need to decide on integrating PM, MM, both, or neither to meet business
needs. We’ll evaluate all four possible business scenarios in the following sections.

7.2 Defining Test Equipment
7.1.1 Scenario 1: PM without MM
In PM, you maintain test equipment as a piece of equipment, hierarchically structured
and assigned to a detailed maintenance plan. This makes it possible to monitor inspec-
tion dates and to create and process maintenance plan orders (e.g., for calibration).
With this option, you create and manage pieces of equipment independently of mate-
rial master data. Because equipment in PM isn’t stock-relevant, business functions of
MM, such as purchase requisition, purchase order, goods receipt, invoice receipt, and
inventory management (storage of equipment), aren’t in scope.
7.1.2 Scenario 2: PM with MM
Implementing this business scenario is the most workload-intensive, but its enormous
benefit is that it enables extensive visibility and availability of information across the
logistics and supply chain management. In this chapter, we’ll be covering this business
scenario so that you have the maximum available information to help you decide
whether it’s worth the time and effort to integrate QM with both PM and MM or just
with one. Because MM is also in scope, the business user can procure and store the test
equipment. Moreover, it’s also possible to serialize and manage as a piece of equip-
ment. This is also the option to synchronize the material master, equipment master,
and serial number.
7.1.3 Scenario 3: MM without PM
With this business scenario, you create test equipment as the material master and pro-
cess all management of purchase requisitions, purchase orders, and goods receipt. Fur-
thermore, the materials that you create also integrate with the different task list types
in the same way as the production resources/tools (PRTs). This business scenario
doesn’t include any of the PM business processes, such as calibration planning, calibra-
tion monitoring, and their documentation.
7.1.4 Scenario 4: Neither MM nor PM
This business scenario has only a restricted management of test equipment as a PRT or
a document master record. Ultimately, it’s available as the where-used list in QM. There
is no calibration planning, execution, or documentation or information availability in
the SAP system, nor does it go through the procurement process available in MM.
7.2 Defining Test Equipment
In quality planning, you can manage test equipment as a PRT, which you can define in
the SAP system by using different types of master records:

7 Integrating with Plant Maintenance
326
 Material master record
 Equipment master record
 PRT master record
 Document master record
Let’s briefly review each of these available options.
7.2.1 Test Equipment as a Material
If you need logistics functions, such as procurement, storage, or quality inspection,
then it makes sense to represent test equipment in the material master records. This
provides all the views of the material master record. The material merely defines the
type of test equipment. This is sufficient for processing purchasing and planning oper-
ations (task lists, inspection plans, etc.) because the individual pieces of test equipment
of a given type usually have the same properties and are therefore interchangeable. For
IM, the individual pieces of test equipment aren’t relevant; rather, it’s the number of
pieces of test equipment that is important.
With the option for serializing materials, the system also provides the option to repre-
sent individual pieces of test equipment. In this case, the material itself corresponds to
a particular configuration for test equipment, and the serial number represents the
individual test equipment.
7.2.2 Test Equipment as PM Equipment
A significantly higher range of functionality is available if you represent the test equip-
ment as equipment in PM. Equipment master records are maintained in PM and allow
you to define individual devices and structure them hierarchically. This means that
you can represent both individual test equipment and combined test equipment or
more complex measuring tools. PM provides comprehensive functions for managing,
monitoring, maintaining, and calibrating the test equipment. When pieces of equip-
ment are included in task lists, you can check whether all the relevant test equipment
is available when production lots are issued.
When material numbers are serialized, the system provides an option for defining and
linking both master records (material master and equipment master) in one process.
First, you enter the material number or select an existing number. Then, you generate
a new serial number using the serialization function. In the subsequent dialog box, you
can then switch to the equipment view, activate the equipment master record, and add
device-specific data. You can generate reports such as results history, graphical trend
analyses, and usage lists.
© 

327
7.3 Configuration Basics
7.2.3 Test Equipment as a Production Resource/Tool
Creating test equipment as a PRT enables you to store information about its status and
location, as well as the standard SAP system management data. You can also group the
test equipment (e.g., measurement equipment, inspection equipment, etc.) or classify
it using the central classification system.
The master record for PRT doesn’t contain a great deal of data, which greatly restricts
the related functionality in the SAP system. In most cases, when you represent test
equipment as a PRT, you maintain only rough master data, while the system doesn’t
support other logistics functions either. For this reason, representing test equipment
as a PRT is the simplest option and doesn’t allow any additional functionality beyond
providing a where-used list.
7.2.4 Test Equipment as a Document
You can use the PRT master record to refer to document data, or you can directly use
the document master records in task lists and inspection plans as a PRT. The interfaces
and functions in document management enable direct access to drawings and other
documents.
The representation of test equipment in document records or the inclusion of docu-
ment records in the other types of PRTs makes it possible to use test equipment in
terms of documents (e.g., drawings, descriptions, etc.). This method is also used primar-
ily for planning and documentation of test equipment usage. It’s characterized by spe-
cial document management functions.
Due to the many alternatives for representing test equipment in the SAP S/4HANA sys-
tem, we suggest that you evaluate every option very carefully on the requirements that
test equipment management should satisfy.
7.3 Configuration Basics
In this section, we’ll cover the minimal configuration steps that you need to integrate
QM with test equipment in PM. Apart from the QM configuration steps that you have
to perform separately at various levels, these configuration steps will help you if you
need to generate QM inspection lots while creating and releasing PM orders.
For this, the first configuration step is to assign the inspection type with the PM inspec-
tion origin. Each piece of test equipment also has a unique serial number that you use
to identify one from another, and you can maintain control of a piece of equipment’s
serial number usage and identification in business processes. If your business process
requires the system to create an inspection lot for a functional location, then you need
to perform only the first configuration step.

7 Integrating with Plant Maintenance
328
7.3.1 Inspection Type Assignment to PM Order Type
To integrate QM with PM so that you can calibrate test equipment using a PM order,
you need to assign inspection type 14 to the relevant PM order and plant combination.
Inspection type 14 of inspection origin 14 (plant maintenance) is specific to handling
QM’s integration with PM and is available as a standard offering in the SAP system. To
assign any configured, specific inspection type of inspection origin 14, use standard
inspection type 14 via menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Inspection 
Inspection Lot Creation  Define Inspections in Plant Maintenance (see Figure 7.2).
In this example, we used the plant 1710 and calibration order YBA2 combination, to
which you assign inspection type 14. Save your settings. During the equipment calibra-
tion process, when you create and then release a calibration order of order type YBA2
for plant 1710, the system will automatically create the necessary inspection lot.
Figure 7.2 Assigning Inspection Type 14 to the Combination of Plant and Order Type
7.3.2 Serial Number Profile
Each piece of test equipment can have a unique serial number that you can use to track
its inventory, as well as its calibration history. You can also control how the system pro-
cesses business transactions of equipment with a serial number by maintaining rele-
vant settings in the serial number profile. To set up a serial number profile, use
Transaction OIS2 or menu path SAP IMG  Plant Maintenance and Customer Service 
Master Data in Management Plant Maintenance and Customer Service  Technical
Objects  Serial Number Management  Define Serial Number Profiles.
Figure 7.3 shows the initial screen for maintaining serial number profiles. You can
either make changes to an existing serial number profile or create a new one. For this
example, use profile 0001, and select the ExistReq. (existing requirement) checkbox,
which ensures that the system checks whether a serial number is created and available
before it allows you to create and test equipment. We’ll show you how these settings
work when we cover the master data creation processes later in this chapter. Set StkCk
(stock check) to 1 so that the system checks for consistency between the material stock
and its serial number. Choose profile 0001 , and then choose Serializing procedures on
the left side, and the screen in Figure 7.4 appears.

329

Figure 7.3 Serial Number Profile
Figure 7.4 Serializing Procedure
Figure 7.4 shows serial number profile 0001, which consists of various functions or pro-
cedures to control business functions using serial numbers in logistics and inventory
management functions. From goods issue and goods receipt to their use in production
and sales functions, you can control a material’s serial number management from an

7 Integrating with Plant Maintenance
330
optional entry to determine whether each serial number should have a corresponding
equipment number.
For the business function or procedure QMSL, for inspection lot maintenance, set the
serial number usage as mandatory (option 03), and an inspection lot for calibration
equipment must also contain a serial number (option 02). You assign this serial num-
ber profile 0001 to the material master of the equipment. This assignment then
ensures that during business processes involving the test equipment, the system refers
to the controls that you maintained in serial number profile 0001. Save your settings.
That’s the entire configuration that you need to undertake. Let’s now delve into creat-
ing the relevant test equipment master data, which will form the basis of running busi-
ness processes and thereby integrating QM and PM.
7.4 Test Equipment Master Data
In the following sections, we’ll discuss how to create important master data in MM, PM,
and QM, while also touching on the integration aspects among them. This master data
will then be subsequently used in business processes or in transactional data.
7.4.1 Create Material Master
To create the material master for the test equipment, which is a PRT, use Transaction
MM01 or menu path Logistics  Quality Management  Test Equipment Management 
Test Equipment  Material  Create. On the initial screen that appears, choose Industry
Type Mechanical and Material Type FHMI Prod. Resources/tools, and then select at least
the following views:
 Basic Data 1
 Purchasing
 Prod.resources/tools
 Plant data / stor. 1
 Plant data / stor. 2
 Quality Management
 Accounting 1
In the Organization Area, choose Plant 1710 and Storage Location 0001, and then
choose Continue.
In the Basic Data view tab, maintain the Description, which in this example is “Lab Test
Equipment”; the Base Unit of Measure as PC; and the Material Group as 001. If you’re
going to procure this calibration equipment, then you need to maintain the relevant
© 

331
7.4 Test Equipment Master Data
entries in the Purchasing view tab of the material master (QM/MM integration was dis-
cussed in Chapter 4). Figure 7.5 shows that the previously configured serial number pro-
file 0001 is assigned to the material master. Doing so makes it possible to use serial
number assignment differently in the various SAP areas (e.g., for finished products and
test equipment). The serial number profile here is set especially for test equipment
monitoring. In addition, for the field SerLevel, enter “1” to enable the system to syn-
chronize equipment number assignment with its serial number.
Figure 7.5 Serial Number Profile 0001 Assignment in Material Master
Figure 7.6 shows the Prod.resources/tools view tab. This is where you enter the task list
usage “009” (all task list types) because you want to include the test equipment in your
inspection plans and task lists. Other information that you enter on this screen has
direct implications on PRT planning and its availability. Selecting any of the check-
boxes makes that specific field a reference field, and you won’t be allowed to make
changes in business transactions.
Save your entries. Creating these views means the setup for the material master for test
equipment is complete. In this example, the system assigns Material 2231 for Plant 1710
for the test equipment (Descr.) Lab Test Equipment.
After creating the material master for calibration equipment, the next step is to main-
tain its serial number.

Figure 7.6 PRT View of Material Master
7.4.2 Material Serial Number
To maintain the serial number of the just created material 2231 (which is the test equip-
ment), use Transaction IQ01 or menu path Logistics  Quality Management  Quality
Planning  Logistics Master Data  Serial Numbers  Create. On the initial screen that
appears, enter material number “2231” in the Material field. If you want to assign a spe-
cific serial number to the material because the test equipment already has a serial num-
ber, enter it in the appropriate field. If you leave this field empty, the system
automatically assigns the next highest number. Finally, you must also enter “Q” in the
Type field to denote that the equipment is test/measurement equipment. Press
(Enter), and the system displays the detailed view for the serial number, as shown in
Figure 7.7. In various available tabs, either the system automatically copies the infor-
mation from material 2231, such as in the ConstType (construction type) field (not
shown), or you can maintain the values, such as for the work center. The system assigns
serial number 10002974 to material 2231.
Tips and Tricks
Using the classification system, you can supplement master data, such as equipment,
material, functional location, and so on, with any fields required for the process flow.
These fields are then available in numerous standard evaluations. During characteris-
tics creation, you can control the permissible values, the input format, and the type of
field (e.g., mandatory or optional entry field).

333
7.4 Test Equipment Master Data
Figure 7.7 Serial Number Creation with Material Number
7.4.3 Test Equipment and Serial Number Synchronization
While maintaining the serial number of a material, you can create the same material as
a piece of equipment. To do so, choose Activate Equipment View, and the screen in
Figure 7.8 appears that shows a three-way combination among material 2231, serial
number 10002974, and equipment 10002974. Maintain the stock-relevant information
of equipment 10002974, such as stock type 01 (for unrestricted stock), plant 1710, and
storage location 0001. Maintaining this information will help the inventory manager
know where it belongs in the store and be able to quickly place the equipment upon
receiving it for maintenance.
Tips and Tricks
When you place the cursor in the Stock type field, the system doesn’t bring up a
dropdown menu for you to choose the relevant stock type, such as unrestricted or
quality inspection. To enter the code that meets your business needs, place the cur-
sor in the Stock type field, and press (F1). In the help that appears, the system dis-
plays the relevant stock types, together with their codes, which you can then use in
this field (Stock type).

Figure 7.8 Equipment Number Synchronization with Serial Number
You get to the Status submenu by choosing the blue i button (at the end of the Status
field). The system displays the permitted status values on the right side of the selection
menu. You can configure the statuses to meet your business requirements. Some pos-
sible status values include the following:
 0001: Test equipment is in storage.
 0002: Test equipment is being used.
 0004: Test equipment is in repair.
 0005: Test equipment is at a contractor location.
Save your entries, and the system creates a material’s serial number, which also syn-
chronizes with the test equipment number.
7.4.4 Test Equipment
To view test equipment with the corresponding serial number, you can also use Trans-
action IE02 or menu path Logistics  Quality Management  Test Equipment Manage-
ment  Test Equipment  Equipment  Change. On the screen that appears, enter
equipment “10002974”, which is the same as serial number 10002974; press (Enter);
and the screen in Figure 7.9 appears.

7.4 Test Equipment Master Data
Figure 7.9 Organization View of Equipment
Here, you can then fill out the details in the Organization tab. In the Account assign-
ment area, you can enter the cost center that the system then books the cost to, and do
so for internal activity allocation for the test equipment. With the appropriate configu-
ration settings in place, the time it takes to calibrate the test equipment can be billed to
this cost center through PM order management. In the Responsibilities area, enter the
Planning Plant, Planner Group, and the responsible work center (Main WorkCtr). These
entries correspond to the entries that you already know from Chapter 2.
Tips and Tricks
To bring about significant business process improvement, you can integrate classifica-
tions with test equipment. Choose Class overview, shown in Figure 7.9, and the system
brings up the classification view, in which you maintain the previously created class of
class type 002 (equipment class) and its characteristics.
Choose the SerData (serial data) tab that is available at the right side of Figure 7.9, and
the screen in Figure 7.10 appears. This screen shows the three-way combination and
data synchronization among Material 2231, Serial Number 10002974, and the Equip-
ment 10002974. When you routinely calibrate this equipment, you can view its calibra-
tion history by choosing History.

7 Integrating with Plant Maintenance
336
Figure 7.10 Material, Equipment, and Serial Number Synchronization
Tips and Tricks
Depending on how deeply you want to go to integrate equipment calibration of PM
with QM, you can also integrate Measuring Points/Counters for test equipment. A
measuring point is the identifier that you use to measure a piece of equipment’s char-
acteristic. This identifier can be, for example, a sensory test, and it maintains its value
at 100. So, after every 100 sensory tests, the sensory test equipment is due for calibra-
tion. With measuring documents, you maintain the actual number of sensory tests
that this equipment performed. A sensory test is one of the tests (others are aroma and
taste) found often in the food industry to measure consumers’ reaction to under-
development or under-trial products. Measuring points also use classification.
7.4.5 General Task List
The SAP S/4HANA system provides two tools for planning test equipment monitoring.
First, it provides the maintenance plan that specifies when and how frequently you
should calibrate test equipment. Second, it provides the general task list that specifies
what tasks to perform during calibration.
© 

337
7.4 Test Equipment Master Data
You need to assign a unique maintenance plan and general task list to every piece of
test equipment. Theoretically, you can assign a common maintenance plan to several
pieces of equipment if they all have exactly the same maintenance date. In this exam-
ple, however, we create a separate maintenance plan for every piece of equipment. In
the same way, you can assign separate general task lists to every piece of equipment. In
this example, we create a shared task list named equipment calibration tasks.
You first need to create a general task list. This is a type of routing that business users
use to perform maintenance and calibration tasks. In some places in the SAP S/4HANA
system, the term task list or PM task list is used. In this section, we provide only limited
information on the required entries. You can create operations for the individual work
steps, assign workstations and PRTs to the operations, schedule setup times and work
times, and enter corresponding costs.
Assume that one general task list suffices for all equipment, which you can then assign
to all maintenance plans from the very beginning. Also assume that there is only one
central calibration point with one workstation. Costs are entered at a flat rate through
cost center accounting and aren’t dependent on calibration duration. This configura-
tion provides you with a relatively easy-to-implement scenario, which you can still
enhance and adapt to changing requirements at any time after a productive start.
To create a general task list, use Transaction IA05 or menu path Logistics  Quality
Management  Test Equipment Management  Calibration Planning  Maintenance Task
List  General Task List  Create. On the initial screen, you don’t have to enter any infor-
mation. The system automatically assigns a group number and a group counter. In this
example, it’s group 40, and the group counter is 1. You can also assign an external
group number if there is any such business need. Similarly, you can enter a key date if
you want the task list to be effective from any specific date. If you don’t enter any date,
the system incorporates the date of general task list creation as the key date (or effec-
tive date).
Press (Enter), and the screen in Figure 7.11 appears, which is the header of the general
task list.
Enter the task list name “Equipment Calibration Tasks” and fill out the other manda-
tory fields, such as Overall Status as 4 (Released) and Usage also as 4 (Plant Mainte-
nance). You can also assign a maintenance strategy that applies to all the equipment to
which this task list is assigned. Any information that you enter on this screen applies to
the entire task list. For example, entering Work Center “RES-0100” and Plant “1710”
automatically copies to all operations of the task list. In the QM Data area, assign
Inspection Points as 300, as the system will refer to it during results recording for
inspection lot. The next step is to create operations (or steps) for the general task list.
Choose Operation, and the screen in Figure 7.12 appears.

Tips and Tricks
You can integrate Document Management System (DMS) for specific operations of a
general task list. Visual instructions help the equipment maintenance or calibration
engineer have access to relevant drawings or specifications that are needed to perform
equipment calibration tasks. Chapter 20 covers DMS.
Choose Activity 0010, and then choose Master Ins. (master inspection characteristic) to
assign inspection characteristics to specific operations of the task list (see Figure 7.13).
Here, you see the operation view in which you can assign the master inspection charac-
teristics and their values, which then become available during results recording. For
our example, enter a quantitative master inspection characteristic with the short text
“Color rays” and with upper and lower limits. Notice that the system offers the options
to maintain comprehensive QM data here. Save your entries.
After saving the general task list, you can create the maintenance plan for the individ-
ual test equipment.
Figure 7.13 Inspection Characteristics Assignment in General Task List

Tips and Tricks
If you need to create a task list that is specific to a piece of equipment, then you can use
Transaction IA01 to create an equipment task list. The principles and fundamentals
that apply to general task lists also apply to equipment task lists, with the difference
that an equipment task list is specific to individual pieces of equipment only.
7.4.6 Maintenance Plan
The purpose of a maintenance plan is to plan maintenance deadlines and cycles for cal-
ibration. Although this example uses time-dependent planning, the system also sup-
ports activity-specific planning (e.g., calibration after 300 uses) or a combination of
both (e.g., check after every three months or 300 uses). In addition, you can assign
order specifications or maintenance strategies. The type of activity is defined using a
reference in the maintenance plan to the corresponding task list. A prerequisite for cre-
ating the maintenance plan is that you’ve already created the test equipment that you
want to calibrate with this maintenance plan, as well as the corresponding general task
list.
To create a maintenance plan, use Transaction IP41 or menu path Logistics  Quality
Management  Calibration Planning  Maintenance Planning  Maintenance Plan  Cre-
ate Single Cycle Plan. On the screen that appears, for Maintenance Plan Category,
choose Maintenance Order. This means that you want the system to create the PM
order (the calibration order) each time the test equipment’s calibration is due. Other
options available are inspection lot creation for stability study, physical samples, PM
notification, and even service orders for the services that the supplier provides.
In the Maintenance plan cycle tab, enter the cycle (frequency) of the calibration inter-
val. This value denotes the frequency with which you need to conduct equipment cali-
bration. Typical values can be three months, six months, or one year. In the screen in
Figure 7.14, enter “365 DAY”. Scroll down so that the screen in Figure 7.15 appears.
In the Reference object area of Figure 7.15, enter the serial and material numbers for the
test equipment in the respective fields. Then, fill out the Task List area with the infor-
mation shown. This is where you create the link between this maintenance plan and
the general task list. If you know the task list type, plan group number, and plan group
counter for your general task list, then you can enter them directly in the respective
fields. Otherwise, you can search for the general task list using the binoculars icon in
the application toolbar and copy the data. In this case, look at Task List Typ A (task list).
You’ve already entered task list type A (general), so enter “40” in Task LstGrp.
If you entered the data completely and correctly in the equipment and if the necessary
settings are in place, the system automatically copies the available data to the Planning
Data area, and you don’t have to make any more entries. However, we suggest that you
pay special attention to the information in the Planning Data area, such as whether the
© 

341
7.4 Test Equipment Master Data
right order type (YBA2 in this example) is there. When the system creates a mainte-
nance call object, it refers to the information that you maintain here. Similarly, if you
set the Do Not Rel. (release) Immediately indicator, the system doesn’t release the cali-
bration order on its creation. Putting this control in place can help business users if
there is a need to evaluate the system-created calibration orders before releasing them
for further processing or action.
Figure 7.14 Maintenance Plan
Figure 7.15 Planning Details in Maintenance Plan

Lastly, you need to set the scheduling parameters. Refer to the Maintenance plan
scheduling parameters tab in the maintenance plan header (see Figure 7.16).
Figure 7.16 Scheduling Parameters of the Maintenance Plan
You can change the testing schedule of maintenance planning. This may be the case
when there is a need to change the testing frequency of calibration equipment. You can
also use this option to enter any missing or incomplete information in the mainte-
nance plan.
Tips and Tricks
You can also use Transaction IP02 to directly make changes to the maintenance plan.
Enter maintenance plan “151” on the initial screen, and press (Enter), and you’re taken
to the screen in Figure 7.16.
Figure 7.16 shows the screen where you can define when the system should include test
equipment requiring calibration in the worklist and when the next cycle for calibration
should start again. For example, the worklist can contain upcoming calibrations that
are due four weeks before the deadline.
A call horizon, defined as a percentage, enables the business process owner to control
when the system creates a call object on its planned or due date. For example, a 0% call
horizon means that as soon as the planned or due date of the call object (which, in this
case, is a calibration order) occurs, the system immediately creates the calibration order.
Similarly, a 90% call horizon means the system will call the object on a time horizon of
90% from the date of the next planned inspection lot creation. Other available options
are how the system should respond when there are deviations between planned
and actual tasks. You can define not only the tolerance for early or late completion in

7.5 Business Processes in Test Equipment Management
The example in this chapter stipulates that the system automatically create a calibra-
tion order of order type YBA2, according to maintenance plan 151. Further, the neces-
sary configuration settings will also ensure that the system automatically creates an
inspection lot of inspection type 14 on release and on saving the calibration order.
Before we get into that process, we’ll also cover the business scenario in which a busi-
ness user needs to inform the maintenance personnel of faulty or defective test equip-
ment.
Figure 7.21 shows that a business user can also create a maintenance request (a PM noti-
fication in the system by using Transaction IW26) to communicate the need to perform
equipment calibration. The business user may also create a PM notification due to
equipment malfunction by using Transaction IW24. All of these scenarios apply when
there is an actual and practical need to calibrate the test equipment instead of waiting
for the system to create calibration orders according to the maintenance plan.
Figure 7.21 Business Processes in Test Equipment Management
The maintenance planner can evaluate the PM notification to see if there is a need to
convert it to a PM order. If so, the maintenance planner can use the PM order creation
option available right in the PM notification creation screen. Alternately, using Trans-
action IW34 enables the maintenance planner to reference the PM notification while
creating a PM order, which is basically converting a PM notification into a PM order. On
release and on saving the PM order, the system automatically creates the QM inspec-
tion lot of inspection type 14. Maintenance engineers can then approach the ware-
house to issue the components or spare parts required for equipment maintenance.
The next quality steps entail recording results and making a usage decision. If PM is to
further integrate with QM, then the business user can perform confirmation of opera-
tions (tasks) performed with Transaction IW31. Finally, the business process ends with
completion of the PM order—both technical and business completion.
Note
There is a great similarity of functions and functionality between PM notification cre-
ation and that of QM notification. If there’s a business need to create a PM notification
before converting it into a PM order, then refer to Chapter 12 on quality notification.

7.5 Business Processes in Test Equipment Management
To start calibrating the test equipment, you first need to select the required line and
release the order using the Release Order function. This creates an inspection lot with
all the data required for calibration inspection. At the same time, the status of the order
is changed to In Process. You can also automate this manual release step with the right
configuration settings.
7.5.5 Calibration Orders Completion
As soon as calibration of the test equipment is complete, you select all the pieces of test
equipment that have the status In Process. Referring once again to the list that you cre-
ated using Transaction IW38 (Section 7.5.4), you use menu path Order  Functions  Com-
plete (Technically) to inform the system that you’ve completed calibration of the
selected test equipment. To fully complete the calibration order, however, you also
need to complete it in business terms through menu path Order  Functions  Complete
(Business). Now the calibration order is fully completed for the SAP system, and the
next planning cycle starts.
Tips and Tricks
If the calibration operation takes a longer (e.g., after being sent to an external calibra-
tion station), you must remember to also set the user status accordingly in the equip-
ment view of the serialized material. Don’t confuse the status of the PM order with the
user status of the equipment.

number of calibration orders; and reported errors. With the results history, you can dis-

You can use the evaluation options for the standard configuration of the SAP S/4HANA

7.6 Inspection Checklists: Inspection Type 8916
While the PM-QM integration has generally been used as a workaround to manage rou-
tine or periodic inspections of technical objects (equipment or functional locations),
SAP has introduced the inspection checklist functionality to process this critical main-
tenance process of results recording in the system in the form of a checklist. Depending
on the configuration settings, the system can even trigger follow-on activities, such as
creating notifications for prompt and timely maintenance.
Inspection checklist is again a PM-QM integration process, and SAP has introduced a
new inspection type, 8914, as well. Further, standard configuration is already predeliv-
ered that can either be used right away or can be used as a reference to create different
checklists.
Apart from results recording and usage decisions undertaken by the maintenance
team, another alternate is using the mobile solution from SAP called SAP Service and
Asset Manager, which is intuitive and more user friendly than using the SAP Fiori and
SAP GUI options available in the SAP S/4HANA system.
The following sections cover the configuration and other prerequisites that need to be
in place for an inspection list, followed by setting up the required master data. This is
then followed by discussing the end-to-end business process of the automatic creation
of an inspection checklist when a maintenance order is released.

and its integration with the material master and serial number. We also briefly dis-
